summary: Describes version 2 of RPCSEC_GSS, which is the same as version 1 from RFC 2203 except that it adds support for channel bindings. RPCSEC_GSS lets remote procedure call protocols use the GSS-API for security. This is a Proposed Standard, later updated by RFC 7861.

plainLanguage.summary: RPCSEC_GSS version 2 is version 1 with one addition: channel bindings. After the two ends set up a secure connection, each proves it knows the same secret information about that connection, which shows that no one is sitting in the middle. Once proven, the per-call checks can be left out.

questions: how does rpcsec_gss v2 stop a man in the middle
subtitle: Adds channel bindings to RPCSEC_GSS so an RPC caller can prove it is on the same secure path as the server.

tldr.problem: RPCSEC_GSS protects each remote call with a message integrity code, even when the network path below it is already secure. That is wasted work, and it does not prove that the two ends share the same channel.
tldr.mechanism: Version 2 adds a new RPCSEC_GSS procedure, RPCSEC_GSS_BIND_CHANNEL, in which each side computes a message integrity code over the shared channel information and sends it to the other. A new service, rpc_gss_svc_channel_prot, then lets requests travel with empty verifiers.
tldr.outcome: Version 2 is a superset of version 1 and keeps the same credential format, with a new version number. It was later updated by RFC 7861.

facts.label: Bind channel result codes
facts.value: 0 OK, 1 prefix not supported, 2 hash not supported

today: RFC 5403 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2009. It updates RFC 2203 and was later updated by RFC 7861.

sections.title: What Version 2 Adds
sections.content:
RPCSEC_GSS version 2 is the same as version 1, specified in RFC 2203, except that support for channel bindings has been added. The primary motivation for channel bindings is to take secure advantage of hardware-assisted encryption that might exist at lower levels of the networking protocol stack, such as at the Internet Protocol layer in the form of IPsec. The secondary motivation is that even if lower levels are no more efficient at encryption than the RPCSEC_GSS layer, encryption happening at the lower level can be redundant at the RPCSEC_GSS level.

RPCSEC_GSS version 1 and version 2 are protocols that exchange tokens emitted by the Generic Security Services framework, and they differ only in the support for GSS channel bindings in version 2. GSS itself supports channel bindings, so in theory version 2 could use native GSS channel bindings. However, not all implementations of all GSS mechanisms support channel bindings, which is sufficient justification for the approach taken here: modify the RPCSEC_GSS protocol to support channel bindings independently of the capabilities of the GSS mechanism being used.

Once an initiator and a target are mutually assured that they are each using the same secure, end-to-end channel, the overhead of computing message integrity codes for authenticating and integrity-protecting RPC requests and replies can be eliminated, because the channel is doing the same job. If the channel also provides confidentiality, the overhead of RPCSEC_GSS privacy protection can be eliminated too. The document also provides the External Data Representation description in a form the reader can extract into a machine-readable file with a short shell script.
sections.plainLanguage: Version 2 differs from version 1 in one way: it can bind the RPC session to the secure channel underneath it. That proves both ends are talking over the same path, and it lets the RPC layer stop repeating work the channel already does.

sections.title: Channel Bindings Explained
sections.content:
If a channel between two parties is secure, there must be shared information between the two parties. This information might be secret or not; the requirement for secrecy depends on the specifics of the channel. For example, the shared information could be the concatenation of the public key of the source and the destination of the channel, where each public key has a corresponding private key.

Suppose the channel is not end-to-end, so a man-in-the-middle exists, with one channel from the initiator to the man-in-the-middle and one from the man-in-the-middle to the target. The man-in-the-middle cannot force each channel to use the same public keys, because a public key derives from a private key and the key management system for each node will assign unique or random private keys. At most, the man-in-the-middle can force one end of each channel to use the same public key, so the integrity code of the public keys from the initiator will not be verified by the target, and the integrity code from the target will not be verified by the initiator.

A higher-layer protocol using the secure channel can safely exploit it if each higher-level party can prove that they each know the channel's shared information, and that the proof is being conveyed by each of them and not by some other entity. RPCSEC_GSS version 2 adds an optional round-trip in which the initiator computes a GSS message integrity code on the channel binding's shared information and sends it to the target. The target verifies it and in turn sends its own message integrity code of the shared information to the initiator, which verifies that too. This accomplishes three things at once: the initiator and target are mutually authenticated, they prove they know the channel's shared information and are thus using the same channel, and the first two happen simultaneously.
sections.plainLanguage: A secure channel hides something both ends know, such as the keys in use. Each end proves it knows that same information, so a man in the middle cannot pass the proof along without the two keys failing to match.

sections.title: The New Version Number
sections.content:
The RPCSEC_GSS version 2 credential has the same format as the version 1 credential, corrected so that the definition is in legal XDR description language, with the field version, a keyword in RFC 1831, replaced by rgc_version. Setting the rgc_version field to 2 indicates that the initiator and target support channel bindings.

The version 2 description adds one value to each of two enumerations. The security service enumeration gains rpc_gss_svc_channel_prot = 4, alongside rpc_gss_svc_none = 1, rpc_gss_svc_integrity = 2 and rpc_gss_svc_privacy = 3, with the value 0 reserved. The procedure enumeration gains RPCSEC_GSS_BIND_CHANNEL = 4, alongside RPCSEC_GSS_DATA = 0, RPCSEC_GSS_INIT = 1, RPCSEC_GSS_CONTINUE_INIT = 2 and RPCSEC_GSS_DESTROY = 3. Two constants are defined, RPCSEC_GSS_VERS_1 = 1 and RPCSEC_GSS_VERS_2 = 2, and the credential union switches on the version number, carrying the same version 1 credential structure for both cases.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing about the shape of the credential changes. Version 2 is signalled by a single field, and it adds one new procedure and one new security service to two lists of numbered values.

sections.title: The BIND_CHANNEL Exchange
sections.content:
Once an RPCSEC_GSS version 2 handle has been established over a secure channel, the initiator MAY issue RPCSEC_GSS_BIND_CHANNEL. Targets MUST support it. Like RPCSEC_GSS_INIT and RPCSEC_GSS_CONTINUE_INIT requests, the NULL RPC procedure is used, but unlike those two requests the arguments of the NULL procedure are not overloaded, because the verifier is large enough for the purpose. The gss_proc field is set to RPCSEC_GSS_BIND_CHANNEL, the seq_num field is set as if gss_proc were RPCSEC_GSS_DATA, the service field is set to rpc_gss_svc_none, and the handle field carries the handle returned by RPCSEC_GSS_INIT or RPCSEC_GSS_CONTINUE_INIT.

The request verifier is the XDR encoding of a structure with three fields. The first is the channel binding prefix, up to but excluding the colon that separates the prefix from the suffix. The second is the object identifier of the hash algorithm used to compute the binding hash. The third is the output of GSS_GetMIC() on the concatenation of the XDR-encoded RPC header and the XDR encoding of a structure holding a hash of the channel bindings. A hash is used rather than the channel bindings themselves because some bindings, such as those composed of public keys, can be relatively large and would place a higher space burden on implementations.

The reply verifier carries a result structure and a message integrity code of its own. The result is a switched union on a status value. The status OK means the target accepted the channel bindings and verified the request's integrity code. The status PREF_NOTSUPP means the target did not support the prefix in the request and returned a list of prefixes it does support, so the initiator can pick its next preferred one. The status HASH_NOTSUPP means the target did not support the hash algorithm in the request and returned a list of object identifiers it does support, with one or more elements. The reply's integrity code covers the sequence number, the hash of the channel bindings and the result, using the hash algorithm the target settled on.
sections.plainLanguage: Once the secure channel is up, the caller may send a BIND_CHANNEL request that carries a hash of the channel's shared information and a code over it. The server checks the code, sends back its own code, and reports whether it accepted the binding.

sections.title: The Channel Protection Service
sections.content:
RPCSEC_GSS version 2 targets MUST support the rpc_gss_svc_channel_prot service. It is valid only if RPCSEC_GSS version 2 is being used, an RPCSEC_GSS_BIND_CHANNEL procedure has been executed successfully, and the secure channel still exists.

When rpc_gss_svc_channel_prot is used, the RPC requests and replies are similar to those of rpc_gss_svc_none except that the verifiers on the request and reply always have the flavor set to AUTH_NONE and their contents are zero length. Even though NULL verifiers are used, non-NULL RPCSEC_GSS credentials are still used, so that the principal sending the request can be identified. The same credential is used as before, except that the service field is set to rpc_gss_svc_channel_prot.

The implementation notes add that once a successful BIND_CHANNEL procedure has been performed on a version 2 context handle, the initiator's implementation may map application requests for rpc_gss_svc_none and rpc_gss_svc_integrity to rpc_gss_svc_channel_prot credentials, and, if the secure channel has privacy enabled, requests for rpc_gss_svc_privacy may be mapped as well.
sections.plainLanguage: With the binding proved, a request no longer needs its own integrity code, because the channel already protects it. The request still carries credentials, so the server knows who sent it.

sections.title: Version Negotiation and Deployment
sections.content:
An initiator that supports version 2 simply issues an RPCSEC_GSS request with the rgc_version field set to RPCSEC_GSS_VERS_2. If the target does not recognize that value, the target returns an RPC error as described in RFC 2203. The initiator MUST NOT attempt to use an RPCSEC_GSS handle returned by version 2 of a target with version 1 of the same target, and MUST NOT attempt to use a handle returned by version 1 with version 2.

To ensure interoperability, implementations of RPCSEC_GSS version 2 SHOULD NOT transfer tokens between the initiator and target that use native GSS channel bindings. On deployment, RPCSEC_GSS version 2 is a superset of version 1 and so can be used in all situations where version 1 is used. Version 2 should be used when the new functionality, channel bindings, is desired or needed.
sections.plainLanguage: An initiator simply asks for version 2. If the server does not understand it, the server refuses and the initiator falls back. Handles from one version must never be mixed with the other.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The base security considerations are those of RFC 2203, those of the channel bindings document, and those of the actual secure channel being used. Even though RPCSEC_GSS_DATA requests that use rpc_gss_svc_channel_prot protection do not involve constructing more GSS tokens, the target SHOULD stop allowing such requests once the GSS context expires.

With channel bindings, it becomes extremely critical that the message integrity code used by the GSS mechanism be difficult to forge. The distinction in seriousness is that for version 1, forging a single code at most lets an attacker inject one bogus request. With version 2 and channel bindings, forging a single code lets the attacker inject bogus requests as long as the channel exists. The RFC walks through that attack: a man-in-the-middle intercepts the initiator's RPCSEC_GSS_INIT message and changes the version number from 1 to 2 before forwarding it to a version 2 target, and changes the reply's version number from 2 to 1 before forwarding it to a version 1 initiator, so neither end notices. The man-in-the-middle then constructs a BIND_CHANNEL request using the integrity code of an RPCSEC_GSS_DATA request and repeats the attempt each time the initiator sends another DATA request, so the probability of a successful forgery rises with every iteration.

Two methods are given to thwart it. The target SHOULD require a stronger integrity code for a BIND_CHANNEL request than for a DATA request, for example the widest possible HMAC the mechanism supports, and if the target expects N DATA requests before the context expires, it SHOULD require an HMAC for BIND_CHANNEL that is log base 2 of N bits longer than it normally requires. If a long enough code is not available, the target could limit the number of DATA requests it allows on the context. Each time the target fails to verify a BIND_CHANNEL integrity code, it SHOULD reduce the lifetime of the underlying GSS context by a significant fraction; a possible heuristic is to halve it each time, so with a context lifetime of 8 hours, or 28800 seconds, 15 failed attempts would destroy the context. A mitigation that was considered and rejected was protecting the version number with the version 2 INIT and CONTINUE_INIT tokens, because that only moves the guessing to the INIT message and there is no way to include the version number in the tokens without changing GSS or the GSS mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: Channel bindings make the integrity code more valuable, so a forged code now buys an attacker more than a single request. The server should ask for a longer code when the binding is set up, and should shorten the life of a session every time a binding check fails, so repeated guessing destroys the session quickly.

messages.label: RPCSEC_GSS_BIND_CHANNEL REQUEST
messages.note: Carries the hash of the channel bindings and an integrity code over it.

messages.label: RPCSEC_GSS_BIND_CHANNEL REPLY
messages.note: Returns the hash and an integrity code the initiator can verify.
